As traditional giants rush into digital dollars, USDD’s Yvonne Chia explains why 24/7 access, self-custody, and transparent yield give decentralized stablecoins an edge banks can’t replicate.

20 November – Road Town, Totorla, British Virgin Islands – Decentralized stablecoin protocol USDD is accelerating its multichain utility across TRON, Ethereum, and BNB Chain—combining automated sUSDD yield via its Smart Allocator with GasFree zero-TRX transfers—as traditional financial giants race to build competing stablecoin rails. 

In a recent industry interview with instant exchange partner ChangeNOW, USDD Head of Communications Yvonne Chia outlined why self-custody, 24/7 settlement, and transparent onchain reserves give decentralized digital dollars a structural advantage over bank-issued alternatives.

1. Permissionless Access vs. Gatekept Accounts

For billions of people globally, opening and maintaining a traditional bank account still involves paperwork, minimum balance requirements, geographic restrictions, and approval delays. Even when banks integrate stablecoin rails behind the scenes, those services remain gated behind legacy compliance walls and intermediary control.

Crypto-native stablecoins flip that model on its head. As Yvonne Chia highlighted during the interview:

“Compare this to a stablecoin like USDD, where all you need is a phone, a working internet connection, you can immediately start a wallet and you have access to your funds right away.”

With USDD, users can access and manage their digital dollars directly through their own wallets, without depending on traditional financial intermediaries. 

This represents a fundamental shift in financial access: users are no longer limited to the services, operating hours, or account structures of a single institution. Instead, they have the freedom to hold, manage, and transfer their assets on their own terms.

Self-custody also gives users greater autonomy over their financial decisions. They can choose which wallets to use, where to transfer their assets, and which supported decentralized applications to interact with, without needing to route every transaction through a centralized financial institution. 

With USDD, users’ digital dollars can move with them across an open blockchain ecosystem, rather than remaining tied to a particular bank or service provider.

2. 24/7 Global Settlement vs. “Banking Hours”

Legacy payment networks still operate on decades-old schedules: weekend cutoffs, bank holidays, and multi-day cross-border settlement delays accompanied by hefty wire fees.

Blockchain networks never close. Whether it is a Sunday night or a public holiday, USDD moves globally without depending on traditional banking operating hours or settlement windows.

“We are able to have transfers 24/7 and we’re not limited to any traditional banking hours. So I think that in some ways, stablecoins are not just becoming banks, but exceeding what traditional banks can offer to users.”

To make everyday transfers even smoother than fintech apps, USDD introduced GasFree integration on TRON, allowing users on supported wallets to pay network fees directly in USDD without needing to hold TRX.

This removes another practical barrier to stablecoin adoption: having to acquire and maintain a separate gas token just to transfer digital dollars. With GasFree, eligible users can pay approximately 0.5 USDD per transaction, compared with around 1.5 USDT for a standard USDT transfer under the referenced fee conditions.

These improvements matter because the usefulness of a stablecoin is not determined by its peg alone. Low-cost transfers, straightforward wallet experiences, and around-the-clock availability are what make digital dollars practical for everyday payments and global value transfers.

3. Passing Yield Back to Users vs. Bank Spreads

Perhaps the sharpest contrast between banks and decentralized stablecoins lies in how yield is distributed. 

In traditional banking, institutions take customer deposits, deploy them into yield-generating markets, and retain a significant portion of the returns. Everyday depositors may receive relatively low interest rates, while higher-yielding products often come with eligibility requirements, minimum deposits, or fixed maturity periods.

Stablecoins introduce another way to participate in digital-dollar opportunities. Rather than keeping capital entirely within a traditional deposit account, users can access onchain yield opportunities through decentralized protocols and transparent investment mechanisms.

USDD was built to return that value directly to holders. Through USDD Earn, users can deposit USDD to receive sUSDD, earning automated, competitive yield powered by our Smart Allocator system, with no fixed lock-up periods restricting access to their capital.

For users, the distinction is important: USDD Earn provides access to a productive stablecoin while maintaining flexibility, rather than requiring users to commit their capital to a conventional fixed-term product.

4. Onchain Verification vs. Institutional Trust

Traditional banks ask customers to trust closed-door balance sheets and periodic regulatory filings—until a crisis proves otherwise. 

USDD takes a different approach through its “Don’t trust, verify” ethos, emphasizing publicly accessible onchain information and independent verification.

  • Onchain Transparency: Smart contract addresses, collateral reserves, and Smart Allocator deployments are publicly viewable, allowing users to examine relevant information directly on the blockchain.
  • Structured Disclosures: Quarterly Treasury Reports provide additional information about reserve positions, financial performance, and operational developments.
  • Independent Security Reviews: USDD undergoes third-party security audits to assess its smart contracts and identify potential vulnerabilities.

Transparency does not eliminate financial or technical risks, but it changes how users can evaluate them. Instead of relying exclusively on an institution’s assurances, users have access to information that can be independently examined and verified.

5. Beyond a Single Network: An Open, Multichain Financial Ecosystem

Financial freedom is not just about holding digital dollars. It is also about being able to use them wherever opportunities and applications exist. A stablecoin confined to a single network or limited use case cannot fully realize the potential of open blockchain finance.

Following its January 2025 protocol upgrade, USDD expanded natively from TRON onto Ethereum and BNB Chain, extending its reach across multiple blockchain ecosystems.

This multichain presence allows USDD to connect with different communities, liquidity environments, and decentralized applications. Its sUSDD product has also expanded into DeFi integrations, including Pendle and Morpho, giving users additional ways to access yield strategies across supported ecosystems.

The bigger picture is an interconnected financial ecosystem in which users can move between holding, transferring, exchanging, and deploying their stablecoins according to their own needs. These are not isolated functions. Together, they make stablecoins more useful as everyday financial infrastructure.

The Future: Interconnected, Open, and Multichain

Banks will undoubtedly continue using stablecoin rails to modernize their back-end settlement. However, true financial freedom comes from open networks where assets flow freely across protocols without intermediaries.

For USDD, the opportunity goes beyond offering a dollar-pegged asset. It is about making digital dollars accessible, transferable, and productive across an interconnected financial ecosystem. From self-custody and 24/7 transfers to flexible yield opportunities and multichain DeFi access, these capabilities give users more ways to put their money to work.

Banks may be bringing stablecoins into traditional finance. Crypto-native protocols are showing what stablecoins can make possible beyond it.

title: Anthropic Stock Drops 10% After Record IPO
summary:
Key Takeaways: Anthropic had fallen under intense selling pressure ahead of the opener on Nov. 20, reversing a portion of its record IPO gains. The stock started the day at
The post Anthropic Stock Drops 10% After Record IPO appeared first on CryptoNinjas.
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Anthropic had fallen under intense selling pressure ahead of the opener on Nov. 20, reversing a portion of its record IPO gains.
  • The stock started the day at $111.50 and ended the first trading day at $97.17, which is 17.07% above its public issue price of $83.
  • Investor mood was hurt by a broader technology sell-off as well as doubts over valuations for AI and chip-built hardware.

Anthropic’s big bid to list on the Nasdaq didn’t have the long-term impact it had hoped for on the AI trade. The company’s stock reversed course in a dramatic fashion after just a day of trading, as investors reevaluated the worth of the cryptocurrency for their AI growth potential.

  • Anthropic Gives Back Gains After Record IPO
  • AI Valuations Face Renewed Investor Scrutiny
    • Broader Technology Selloff Adds Pressure

Anthropic Gives Back Gains After Record IPO

In its initial public offering on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Nov. 19, under the ticker ANT, Anthropic priced its stock at $83 per share. It sold a total of 980 million shares, with underwriters taking up an option to buy a further 147 million.

That was the broadest IPO ever and netted about $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, according to the company’s November 20 announcement. The first time it was in the market, it had quite heavy acceptance. Shares started at $111.50, about 34 percent higher than the offering price, and peaked at $115.10 during the day.

The rally, however, resumed its momentum through the sell-off during the session. ANT had ended up at $97.17 on Thursday, up 17.07% of its offer price but down almost 13% from the opening price.

Sales at the start of Friday have been underway. The shares last stood at $88.24, just 9% lower than Thursday, Reuters reported. The snaps of other stocks were also below 10%, at various points during the premarket buying and selling, emphasizing the volatility in the share price of this stock.

AI Valuations Face Renewed Investor Scrutiny

The turnaround is more than just a profit-taking move after a first chart at the box office that was unusually strong. Investors also have doubts about whether the massive investment in building AI models and infrastructure will pay off at their current prices.

Various questions were raised about whether Anthropic could continue to trade at about 40 times its total revenue over the prior year, Reuters reported. 

Read More: Anthropic’s $83 IPO Fuels Hyperliquid Bets and Fresh Ether Liquidity Debate Before Nasdaq

Broader Technology Selloff Adds Pressure

At the same time, the release of Anthropic coincided with a poor day for U.S. stocks. The Nasdaq Composite declined 2.25 percent, the S&P 500 edged down 2.02 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 2.19 percent on Thursday.

The pressure appear to have transcended Anthropic as major technology and semiconductors stocks tumbled as well. Several chipmakers suffered further declines as both Nvidia and Metaverse lost over 3% on Friday. 

Market reaction has left doubts about whether an IPO of sorts may rebuild investor faith in the area as investors continue to worry around high valuations, financing, infrastructure future, etc.

The initial trading day or days of Anthropic will thus be an early sign of how well AI stocks are received by the public market. The first reaction was strong enough, but the sudden turnaround highlights how much investors still want more than just a splash than a high-profile listing.

title: U.S. Treasury Secretary Pushes Back on Bigger Fed Hike
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

U.S. Treasury Secretary Pushes Back on Bigger Fed Hike
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged the Fed not to embrace a bigger rate hike as Citi and traders still see a quarter-point move in December and bitcoin fell below $60,000.
This post U.S. Treasury Secretary Pushes Back on Bi...
content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a bigger Federal Reserve rate hike, even as bitcoin broke below $60,000 for the first time since July and stocks sank on bets that the Fed will keep tightening into a selloff.

Bessent told CNBC he would encourage the Fed not to embrace a half-point increase at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. He cited the energy supply shock and a drop in crude prices as reasons for the central bank to hold back.

Bessent says the Fed should look forward

He argued that one governor now backing a 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year. Bessent said it “seems somewhat peripatetic” to want the bigger increase only 11 or 12 months later. He did not name the governor.

“I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards,” Bessent said.

The comments came two days after Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC a half-point hike is probably necessary in December and that the central bank may need to “shock people.” Waller said inflation is “headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”

Fed officials split on how far to go

Waller is not alone. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a quarter-point hike in December, and two floated a larger one. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also declined to rule out a bigger move on Thursday.

“We’ve now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress,” Goolsbee told reporters. “So everything’s always on the table.”

Not everyone wants to go bigger. New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.” St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027.

The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years and held them steady in October. Inflation has stayed hot since the Iran strikes pushed up energy prices earlier this year.

Citi and traders still see a quarter-point hike

Citi still expects a quarter-point increase in December. Global chief economist Nathan Sheets said Thursday he does not see a need for 50 basis points despite persistent inflation. In a note Friday, the bank wrote that “Fed officials will consequently have little appetite to hike into an equity sell-off.”

Citi expects the Fed to hold after December and begin cutting later in 2027. Traders agree on the next step: the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point hike, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 10 basis points to 4.95% as investors bought bonds.

Stocks fell for another day. The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 2% in morning trading, and the VIX volatility index topped 30, its highest level since March.

What it means for bitcoin

Bitcoin traded near $59,700 shortly before 11 a.m. ET, down more than 5% on the day, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro. It broke below $60,000 for the first time since early July and is on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2022.

Higher rates are a headwind for assets that pay no yield, and the selloff has reached companies that hold bitcoin. Strategy’s stock fell for a sixth straight session on Thursday, and the bitcoin price has dropped roughly 25% in a month, a slide Bitcoin Magazine tracked earlier this week.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill tied the outlook to inflation in a note dated Nov. 18. “Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he said.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,300.

Micah Zimmerman

Micah first discovered Bitcoin in 2018 but remained a skeptic on the sidelines for too long. Since 2021, he has covered crypto and business and now works as a news reporter for Bitcoin Magazine, based in North Carolina.

title: Bitcoin (BTC) Price Today: Glassnode Warns of Holder Losses as BTC Approaches Critical $61K Support
summary: Bitcoin (BTC) fell toward $61,000 on November 20 as spot Bitcoin ETF outflows and weaker risk appetite kept pressure on the market.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: BTC

Bitcoin (BTC) fell toward $61,000 on November 20 as spot Bitcoin ETF outflows and weaker risk appetite kept pressure on the market.

Glassnode data also points to a shrinking profit margin for the average Bitcoin holder, raising concerns that another decline could push the market into an unrealized-loss phase.

Fundamental Analysis

Bitcoin faced several sources of selling pressure during the November 17–19 period. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded combined net outflows of approximately $1.13 billion, suggesting that institutional demand weakened as market conditions deteriorated. Expectations of a tighter Federal Reserve stance and weakness across technology stocks added to the cautious mood surrounding risk assets.

Bitcoin (BTC) price chart. Source: Brave New Coin

Derivatives activity further intensified the decline. CoinGlass recorded approximately $201.51 million in Bitcoin derivatives liquidations over the preceding 24 hours. Long positions accounted for $167.97 million, compared with $33.55 million in short liquidations. The imbalance indicates that traders positioned for higher prices absorbed most of the losses as BTC continued to fall.

The average funding rate also turned slightly negative, reflecting a shift in derivatives positioning. However, the liquidation figures do not yet establish that the market has reached a capitulation phase. Instead, they show that bullish positions faced greater pressure during the latest decline.

Liquidity conditions provide another concern. The shrinking supply of stablecoins points to a weaker pool of available capital across the crypto market. With ETF withdrawals accelerating and liquidity declining, Bitcoin may struggle to sustain a recovery without renewed spot demand.

Glassnode Highlights a Narrow Profit Margin

On-chain data from Glassnode shows that Bitcoin remains above its realized price, meaning the average holder is still marginally in profit. However, the MVRV ratio, which compares Bitcoin’s market value with its realized value, has moved close to the breakeven level of 1.

The chart highlights MVRV hovering near breakeven 509 days before the projected April 2028 Bitcoin halving, mirroring patterns observed in previous pre-halving cycles. Source: Glassnode via X

The reading is particularly significant because it suggests that the average investor has limited unrealized gains to absorb further price declines. As of November 2026, the MVRV ratio was only slightly above 1, leaving holders increasingly exposed to a move below their aggregate cost basis.

A fall beneath that threshold would place the average Bitcoin holder in an unrealized-loss position for the first time since early 2023. Such a shift could increase selling pressure, particularly if investors decide to reduce exposure rather than wait for a potential recovery.

Glassnode’s historical comparison also places the current reading approximately 509 days before the estimated April 2028 Bitcoin halving. Previous market cycles experienced periods when MVRV approached breakeven levels ahead of their respective halvings. However, the indicator alone does not establish whether the current market will follow the same pattern.

Technical Analysis

Bitcoin’s technical structure remains firmly bearish despite signs that the market may be approaching an oversold condition. TradingView’s Bitstamp feed placed BTCUSD near $61,368 in the latest available snapshot, representing a decline of approximately $2,396, or 3.76%.

BTCUSD has reached the lower boundary of a previous support zone, with oversold RSI and an extended gap from the EMA stack indicating potential for a modest rebound. Source: KrisadaYoonaisil on TradingView

The aggregated technical summary showed 14 sell signals, nine neutral readings and only three buy signals. Moving averages accounted for most of the negative readings, with 13 sell signals against one neutral and one buy. This configuration reflects the extent of the recent decline and confirms that the BTC price remains below its major trend indicators.

The Relative Strength Index (RSI) stood at 20, placing it deep in oversold territory. The Stochastic indicator also dropped to 3, while the Williams Percent Range reached -99. These readings suggest that selling has become unusually intense over the short term.

Other indicators present a mixed picture. The Commodity Channel Index (CCI) generated a buy signal at -117, while Momentum also indicated a possible rebound. However, the MACD remained bearish at -4,596, and the Average Directional Index (ADX) stood at 43, indicating that the prevailing trend remains strong.

The moving-average structure reinforces the downside bias. The 10-day exponential moving average (EMA) was near $65,713, while the 20-day EMA stood around $69,611. Longer-term averages were also considerably higher than the current market price. This wide separation indicates that Bitcoin has experienced substantial downward momentum and would need sustained buying interest to reclaim those levels.

$61K Support Remains Critical

The immediate focus is on Bitcoin’s ability to defend the $61,000 area, which coincides with a major daily demand zone identified in the TradingView analysis. The sharp bearish impulse has brought BTC close to this region, making its reaction there important for determining the next short-term move.

The deeply oversold indicators and the distance from the major moving averages leave room for a relief bounce. However, oversold conditions do not guarantee an immediate reversal, particularly when the broader trend remains negative.

According to eLs-Trading on TradingView, traders should avoid trying to identify the exact bottom and wait for confirmation before acting around the demand zone. The analysis states: “Never chase or predict the bottom. Always wait for clear confirmation signals to validate the zone before entering.”

If Bitcoin stabilizes above $61,000, the first important upside reference is around $65,500. A recovery toward $69,000 would represent the next resistance test. A sustained move above that level could improve the technical structure, although the broader moving-average configuration would still require attention.

Conversely, a decisive break below $61,000 could expose the previous low near $57,700. The classic S3 pivot level around $58,181 provides another downside reference within the same broader price region.

For now, Bitcoin’s near-term direction depends on whether buyers can defend the $61,000 support area and generate enough demand to counter continued selling. Improving ETF flows and stronger spot-market participation would provide clearer evidence of recovery. Without those developments, the combination of weak liquidity, negative market sentiment and bearish moving averages continues to leave the BTC price vulnerable to further declines.

title: Bitcoin Price Crashes to $59,000 as Market Selloff Deepens
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

Bitcoin Price Crashes to $59,000 as Market Selloff Deepens
Bitcoin fell below $60,000 for the first time since early July on Friday as a tech stock rout, rate hike bets and record ETF outflows hit risk assets.
This post Bitcoin Price Crashes to $59,000 as Market Selloff Deepens fir...
content:
The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower.

Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data. The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000.

The break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss.

Stocks and rate hike bets drive the selloff

Wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower.

Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry.

Rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed. Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield.

Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin.

Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027.

ETF outflows and liquidations

Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week.

Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them.

The move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday.

Crypto stocks fall harder than bitcoin price

Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session. Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading.

Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13.

Data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure.

The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600.

title: US Senate advances prediction market restrictions with DEATH BETS Act
summary: The Senate-approved bill would ban prediction market contracts tied to war, assassination and death amid concerns over potential insider trading on military events.
content:
The US Senate passed legislation Thursday that would prohibit federally regulated prediction markets from offering contracts tied to war, terrorism, assassination and events primarily determined by a person’s death, sending the bill to the House for consideration.

The DEATH BETS Act, introduced by Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff in March, passed by voice vote on Thursday after lawmakers adopted an amendment by unanimous consent. The bill would amend the Commodity Exchange Act to prohibit CFTC-registered exchanges from listing or clearing contracts tied to the specified events.

The legislation also covers contracts referencing US military operations and gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority to identify similar activities that would fall under the ban. Contracts would also be prohibited if, at the time of listing, they are reasonably expected to be settled primarily based on an individual’s death.

The bill was first introduced in March amid insider-trading concerns after six Polymarket traders reportedly earned $1 million betting on the timing of US strikes against Iran. Several wagers were placed just hours before the first reported explosions in Tehran, raising suspicions that traders may have had access to nonpublic information.

When introducing the bill, Schiff warned that allowing traders to profit from violent events could encourage the misuse of classified information, threaten national security and create incentives for violence.

The bill now moves to the House of Representatives, where it must pass before being sent to President Donald Trump for his signature.

title: Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet Exits After Nine Years, Warns AI Is Changing Crypto Security
summary:
Key Takeaways: Charles Guillemet, CTO will be exiting the company at the end of 2026. He contributed to the development of Ledger Donjon and the bolstering of the company’s crypto-security
The post Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet Exits After Nine Years, Warns AI Is Changing Crypto Security appeared fir...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Charles Guillemet, CTO will be exiting the company at the end of 2026.
  • He contributed to the development of Ledger Donjon and the bolstering of the company’s crypto-security measures.
  • As cyber-attack capability exceeds that of defenders, Guillemet said that AI is making it faster, cheaper, and easier to scale.

Charles Guillemet, the Chief Technology Officer at the company, is set to depart at the end of 2026, ending a decade-long tenure at a crypto hardware wallet stalwart like Ledger.

The timing is coming after security threats have become more sophisticated, where artificial intelligence is an ally both to defenders and attackers.

  • Guillemet Leaves After Building Ledger’s Security Operation
    • AI Is Changing the Crypto Security Threat Model
  • Departure Comes During Ledger Hardware Tampering Investigation
    • Guillemet Plans a New Security Venture

Guillemet Leaves After Building Ledger’s Security Operation

Guillemet became CTO after joining Ledger in December of 2017 as its chief security officer. One of his greatest achievements was establishing Ledger Donjon, the internal security and attack research laboratory of the company.

The Donjon has tested hardware, software and infrastructure vulnerabilities as well as studied secure boot systems, post-quantum cryptography and AI assisted security.

Ledger has now sold over 8 million hardware signers in 180 countries protecting about 20% of global crypto assets, Guillemet said. There are more than 100 financial institutions and brands that use the Ledger Enterprise platform as well.

Read More: Binance CFO Kaiser Ng Exits After 5 Years, Justin Yek Takes Over Finance Leadership

AI Is Changing the Crypto Security Threat Model

One of the big aspects of Guillemet’s walking away speech was the increasing importance of AI in cybersecurity.

AI is making attacks faster, cheaper and more scalable, he said. The same technology that Ledger’s Donjon employs to find vulnerabilities can be weaponed by attackers to automate reconnaissance, exploit weaknesses, and attack users at large scale.

This is a bigger problem for the cryptocurrency customers. Hardware wallets will be based on the premise that computers and phones can be hacked, but AI is improving the effectiveness of social engineering, malware creation and automated attacks.

The security-related issue that has kept Ledger busy for years within the crypto industry is gaining traction among companies, governments and autonomous AI agents, Guillemet said.

Departure Comes During Ledger Hardware Tampering Investigation

Guillemet’s announcement comes as a response to Ledger’s investigation of the purchase of real hardware wallets that were altered out of the company’s control.

The malware was installed in some devices distributed via third-party channels, according to Ledger. The implants were created to take in the recapture expressions at the time of formulating a wallet. The company pointed out that it had not been compromised by its Secure Element chip, operating system and servers.

The devices identified as affected or suspected are here in Southeast Asia or Berlin and Dubai, according to Ledger. The company is still looking into the distribution chain and has urged customers to reach out to official support in case they are worried.

Guillemet Plans a New Security Venture

Taking his exit two months later, Guillemet said his employees, vendors, and roadmaps have been well planned for the months prior.

He did not reveal any specifics of the company he is launching, but states he is creating something new and will be targeting new security issues. There has been no reported link between his resignation and the investigation into hardware tampering by Ledger.

title: Bitcoin price drops to $60K as Anthropic drops to $87 in tech sell-off
summary: Bitcoin price strength felt pressure from falling US equities as traders reassessed AI prospects after Anthropic’s IPO.
content:
Bitcoin dropped to $60,000 after Friday’s Wall Street open as crypto markets endured contagion from a fresh rout in tech stocks.

Key points:

  • Bitcoin failed to recover after hitting new 20-week lows of $60,000 as a tech-stock rout gathered momentum.
  • Anthropic stock reached lows of $87.27 on Friday as enthusiasm faded over its record IPO.
  • Analysis warned of multiple macroeconomic headwinds set to keep BTC price strength down going forward.

Nasdaq Composite Index dips to new seven-month low

Data from TradingView showed Bitcoin (BTC) circling $60,000, its lowest levels in 20 weeks.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

US stocks saw continued weakness after reversing during Thursday’s trading session, with Anthropic’s debut on the Nasdaq insufficient to preserve upside momentum. ANT reached highs of $115 before reversing below the $100 mark, falling as low as $87.27 at the time of writing.

Anthropic stock five-minute chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index opened 1.2% lower, reaching 23,517 points — its lowest level since mid-April.

Nasdaq Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

In analysis on the day, crypto trading company QCP Capital drew attention to the lack of momentum in tech stocks despite Anthropic’s record IPO.

“Even Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO failed to restore confidence. Despite opening 34% above its offer price, shares faded to close up just 17%, highlighting a market increasingly unwilling to chase AI valuations,” it wrote.

QCP said that financing concerns remained throughout the AI sector in particular, with markets remaining highly sensitive to that topic throughout 2026.

“AI has become more than an equity growth story. It is increasingly a credit and liquidity story,” it continued.

“As infrastructure spending becomes more dependent on debt financing, weaker investor appetite could push borrowing costs higher, tighten financial conditions and trigger broader deleveraging.”

Related: Bitcoin nears repeat of chart pattern that preceded 2023’s $25K retest

Hawkish Fed policy seen holding Bitcoin back

A flight to safety among investors saw stock markets turn lower across the board and US bond yields drop in step. The 10-year yield fell as low as 4.96% on Friday, its lowest level since Nov. 10.

US 10-year bond yield one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

A speech by Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller at the 2026 College Fed Challenge in Washington, D.C. delivered no new signals on future policy and resulted in yields reversing as traders focused on existing hawkish cues. Earlier this week, Waller told CNBC that he considered a 50-basis-point interest-rate hike in December necessary — twice the current market expectation of 25 basis points.

In his latest analysis, economist Mohamed El-Erian expressed surprise that yields had not fallen further.

“Reflecting this week’s sharp fall in stocks, where a seventh straight day of S&P 500 losses would mark its longest losing streak since 2020, the yield on the 10-year Treasury has pulled back to 4.97%,” he wrote in a blog post.

“While the direction aligns with conventional correlations, the relatively modest size of this week’s yield move down is less typical.”

S&P 500 one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

QCP, meanwhile, saw Bitcoin price performance improving only from a combination of tech-stock stabilization, reduced volatility in rates and the return of institutional capital.

“Until then, short-covering rallies may struggle to develop into sustained upside, particularly if the Fed remains committed to tightening,” it summarized.

title: Coinbase Targets 2027 Launch for In-House Prediction Markets: Bloomberg
summary: Coinbase reportedly plans to introduce its own prediction market contracts in the first half of 2027, potentially reducing its reliance on Kalshi as event-based trading becomes an increasingly important source of revenue. Coinbase is reportedly preparing to launch its own prediction market contracts...
content:
Coinbase reportedly plans to introduce its own prediction market contracts in the first half of 2027, potentially reducing its reliance on Kalshi as event-based trading becomes an increasingly important source of revenue.

Key Takeaways

  • Coinbase reportedly plans to launch its own prediction market contracts in the first half of 2027, giving it greater control over available markets and revenue.
  • Prediction markets have become a rapidly growing business for Coinbase, surpassing a $200 million annualized net revenue run rate in Q3 2026 via partner Kalshi.
  • Industry trading volumes continue to surge, with Kalshi recording $4.15 billion in volume during the Nov. 3 midterm elections and weekly crypto prediction market volume reaching $2.7 billion in October.

Coinbase is reportedly preparing to launch its own prediction market contracts in the United States during the first half of 2027, a move that would give the cryptocurrency exchange greater control over a rapidly expanding business currently powered by its partnership with Kalshi.

According to a Bloomberg report published Thursday, citing a person familiar with the plans, Coinbase intends to offer the contracts to both retail and institutional traders. Developing its own products would allow the company to determine which events are available for trading while retaining a larger portion of transaction revenue.

A Coinbase spokesperson declined to confirm the reported timeline, referring Bloomberg to the company’s previously announced plans to expand its prediction market services and develop its own clearing infrastructure.

The initiative builds on several moves Coinbase has made to establish itself in the sector. In December 2025, the exchange announced an agreement to acquire prediction market startup The Clearing Company. Coinbase also operates a regulated derivatives exchange and received approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for its own clearinghouse in September 2026.

As Bitcoin.com News previously reported, Coinbase launched prediction markets nationwide on Jan. 28 through its partnership with Kalshi. The initial offering included contracts covering cryptocurrency prices, elections, sporting events, economic indicators, entertainment, and weather.

That business has since become one of the exchange’s fastest-growing offerings. During the third quarter of 2026, Coinbase’s prediction market operation surpassed a $200 million annualized net revenue run rate, according to its earnings presentation. Revenue from the product grew at an average quarterly compound rate of 82%, while the average number of daily prediction market traders increased more than 60% from the preceding quarter.

Coinbase Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas described prediction markets as one of the company’s fastest-growing new revenue products. The exchange has also emphasized that the contracts provide a revenue stream less directly dependent on cryptocurrency price volatility.

More than half of the prediction contracts traded through Coinbase during the third quarter involved non-sports events, reflecting demand beyond the category that has helped drive the industry’s explosive growth.

Prediction Market Trading Reaches New Heights

Coinbase’s expansion comes as trading activity across the prediction market industry reaches unprecedented levels.

Bitcoin.com News recently reported that Kalshi recorded $4.15 billion in notional trading volume during the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, its busiest weekday on record. That figure nevertheless fell short of the platform’s $5.3 billion daily record set on Oct. 24. Election-related contracts attracted substantial activity, although sports and other markets continued to account for most trading.

Cryptocurrency prediction markets have also experienced a surge. In late October, weekly notional trading volume for crypto-related contracts across Kalshi and Polymarket reached a record $2.7 billion, according to Bitcoin.com News reporting. Short-duration bitcoin price contracts accounted for much of that activity, demonstrating how prediction markets are increasingly competing with traditional crypto trading products.

The industry’s expansion has also attracted substantial investment and competition. Both Kalshi and Polymarket have pursued multibillion-dollar valuations, while established financial and cryptocurrency companies increasingly view event contracts as an opportunity to diversify their businesses.

However, regulatory disputes threaten to complicate those ambitions.

State authorities have challenged prediction market operators over contracts they contend constitute unlicensed gambling, particularly those tied to sports. On Nov. 12, for example, a Louisiana judge issued a temporary restraining order against 31 entities associated with prediction markets, including Coinbase, Kalshi, Polymarket, and Robinhood.

Coinbase has argued that event contracts fall under the CFTC’s existing federal derivatives authority rather than a patchwork of state gambling regulations—and the CFTC has argued that it has exclusive jurisdiction over such products. The exchange previously urged regulators to maintain a consistent national framework for the growing industry.

For Coinbase, developing an in-house prediction market offering would represent another step toward becoming a broader financial trading platform. It could also position the company to compete more directly with Kalshi, even as the two maintain their existing commercial relationship.

title: Assume You Will Be Hacked: UK Regulators Seek Clean-Slate Recovery Plans for Investment Firms
summary:
UK financial regulators published a joint consultation paper warning finance and investment firms about escalating cyber threats fueled by artificial intelligence and complex supply chains. 
While no new rules are introduced at this stage, the guidance, proposed by the Financial Conduct Authority (F...
content:
2026-11-20T17:40:00.000+02:00

Friday, 20/11/2026 | 15:40 GMT by Tanya Chepkova

  • Regulators estimate UK financial data breaches cost around £200 million annually, with AI accelerating attack speeds.
  • Chief Operations Officers face direct accountability for cyber resilience, and cyber insurance won't shield boards from weak controls.

UK financial regulators published a joint consultation paper warning finance and investment firms about escalating cyber threats fueled by artificial intelligence and complex supply chains.

While no new rules are introduced at this stage, the guidance, proposed by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and the Bank of England, may be used to evaluate investment firms' response to the cyber threats.

“Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats,” said Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA. “Our response doesn’t always have to be making new rules. Firms have asked us to clarify what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides that clarity.”

C-Suite Takes the Heat for Cyber Gaps

The new cyber playbook will apply to PRA-designated investment firms, UK-recognised investment exchanges, and large FCA-regulated brokers subject to SYSC 15A operational resilience rules, and, starting from October 25, 2027, qualified cryptoasset companies.

Smaller brokers outside this regulatory perimeter and UK branches of overseas firms are out of scope, but regulators would encourage them “to refer to it in their cyber risk and resilience management”.

Under the proposed framework, cyber risk becomes a strategic business risk, meaning it would become a direct responsibility of a specified top manager, such as the Chief Operations Officer.

Furthermore, regulators expect entire boards to maintain collective cyber literacy rather than relying on a single technical specialist. Buying a cyber insurance policy would no longer protect the leadership from weak controls.

AI Fuels £200M Breach Threat

UK watchdogs warn that AI is advancing faster than anticipated, amplifying the speed, scale, and sophistication of cyberattacks.

The regulator analysed 33 reported cyber incidents involving UK financial services companies and calculated an illustrative annual cost of approximately £200 million.

This figure is based on IBM’s estimated average cost of £6.05 million for a UK financial services data breach and used as a benchmark rather than a verified amount of losses among the regulated entities.

For investment firms and brokers, exposure is magnified by heavy reliance on third-party software, cloud providers, and external liquidity or data vendors, where a single compromised supplier can trigger a chain reaction across trading venues.

Rebuilding From Scratch Under Fire

Companies should brace for the worst and operate under the assumption that a breach will occur, regulators said.

“Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and severe,” noted Katharine Braddick, Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation at the Bank of England and CEO of the PRA. “Regulators need confidence not just that firms have strong controls, but that they can detect, contain and recover quickly when incidents happen.”

To achieve this, investment firms must pre-define a “minimum level of service” to keep critical operations running in a degraded state and test their ability to execute a “bare metal recovery”.

Basically, they should be able to rebuild their core systems from scratch in a clean environment without relying on potentially compromised backups.

This is especially relevant for trading companies and payment providers, where even a few hours of downtime might ruin reputation and cost a company millions of pounds.

The consultation remains open for industry feedback until February 26, 2027. To ease the compliance burden on global players, UK watchdogs confirmed that international investment firms can use their existing compliance with the EU’s DORA or the US NIST framework as supporting evidence to meet London’s expectations.

title: DBS bets it can lose the deposit and keep the client
summary: The Singapore bank earned a record $208 million in transaction services fees in the third quarter — now it’s helping companies turn deposits into stablecoins they can spend without it.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 20, 2026

The Singapore bank earned a record $208 million in transaction services fees in the third quarter — now it’s helping companies turn deposits into stablecoins they can spend without it.

If a supplier wants USDC on a Sunday, an eligible company can now get Circle’s stablecoin directly from DBS.

That gives the bank a conversion option its client might otherwise take to a crypto exchange. If the treasurer needs to move dollars between the company’s Singapore and US accounts that weekend, DBS can also handle that through its new tokenized deposit link with JPMorgan.

Once the company holds USDC, its treasurer can pay the next invoice without involving DBS. For shareholders, the payoff depends on how often that treasurer comes back, what DBS earns when the money moves and how much operating cash the company leaves on deposit.

Related: Binance hacker moves nearly $600M in ETH, routes funds through THORChain, Chainflip

The Monetary Authority of Singapore issued 100 million Singapore dollars ($77.6 million) of four-week bills on Nov. 6, and the dealers paid in wholesale Singapore dollar central bank digital currency. Here DBS participated as a securities dealer. MAS plans to expand trials in 2027 to explore how institutions could use the bills as collateral.

DBS’s quarterly results put a figure on the business it has to defend. Transaction services generated a record 268 million Singapore dollars in fees in the third quarter, up 8% from a year earlier, before either November deal.

title: Michael Saylor Doubles Down on STRC Buybacks Below $100
summary:
Key Takeaways: Strategy to continue accumulating STRC as long as it is under $100. Saylor noted STRC had the highest daily volume in the $600 million range. A buy-back decreases
The post Michael Saylor Doubles Down on STRC Buybacks Below $100 appeared first on CryptoNinjas.
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Strategy to continue accumulating STRC as long as it is under $100.
  • Saylor noted STRC had the highest daily volume in the $600 million range.
  • A buy-back decreases the number of preferred shares on the books and the payment of future preferred dividends.

Michael Saylor reiterates Strategy’s intention to buy STRC at its stated value of $100 after it swelled more than $600 million in trading volume.

The policy sits within Strategy’s capital strategy for Bitcoin assets, that includes preferred securities, common-stock and selective BTC sales, to help manage liquidity and funding requirements.

  • Saylor Reaffirms STRC Buybacks Below $100
  • STRC Carries a 12% Dividend Rate
    • Strategy Spends $228 Million on Recent STRC Buybacks
    • STRC Sits Inside Strategy’s Bitcoin Capital Structure

Saylor Reaffirms STRC Buybacks Below $100

Saylor said on Nov. 19 that STRC traded more than $600 million in the previous session and was the only one of 456 U.S.-listed income preferred securities to reach that level this year.

$STRC traded over $600M yesterday, the only one of 456 U.S.-listed income preferreds to do so this year. We intend to keep buying below $100. Repurchases facilitate liquidity and lower dividend obligations. We believe they strengthen the credit and benefit common shareholders.

— Michael Saylor (@saylor) November 19, 2026

He also said he expects Strategy to continue purchasing STRC at prices under $100 as repurchases can help to free up future funds while providing liquidity.

The policy was officially launched in July. However the company said that it would have to become more aggressive in the buying as STRC sold at deeper discounts and slowly when the price was at $100.

Read More: MSCI Cuts Strategy From Global Indexes, Putting Bitcoin Treasury Model Under Pressure

STRC Carries a 12% Dividend Rate

STRC is Strategy’s perpetual preferred stock with the stated dividend rate of 12% per annum.

The dividend rate is one of the factors used in Strategy’s strategy to hold the security trading near its posted price of $100. The rate goes through a regular review and is subject to approval of the board.

Repurchasing shares at less than $100 enables Strategy to redeem preferred obligations at a discount. After removal of those shares, the company is not required to pay future dividends on those shares.

This can reduce the short-term cash cost to common shareholders, but will also depend greatly on the funding source of the repurchase.

Strategy Spends $228 Million on Recent STRC Buybacks

Strategy revealed on Nov. 16 that it purchased approximately $228 million worth of STRC during the week, in addition to acquiring 485 BTC. Over the years, the firm has relied on common-stock sales and other funds it has available to finance preferred share repurchases.

Its policy also allows for sale of Bitcoins under some conditions. In Strategy’s third quarter, it sold approximately USD $431.8 million of BTC to finance parts of its preferred dividends and STRC repurchases.

This establishes an important connection between STRC and Strategy’s Bitcoin treasury model: funds raised or generated from various book-of-business segments can be repurposed for non-voting liabilities.

STRC Sits Inside Strategy’s Bitcoin Capital Structure

The STRC is one of several securities Strategy employs to fund and control its Bitcoin-rich balance sheet.

The preferred stock would have a priority over common equity and it would result in a recurring dividend liability. Purchasing it back at less than par diminishes that claim and the more MSTR shares that can be issued to pay for purchases, the more common shares become outstanding.

According to Strategy, its target for STRC is to reach $100 with a high level of liquidity and low volatility.

title: Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food
Block’s first bitcoin payments report found the median Square payment is about $13, with 72% at food and drink businesses, as it pushes for a de minimis tax exemption.
This post Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on S...
content:
Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block said in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.

The report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29.

Food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period.

“Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the company wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy.

Coffee, quick bites and repeat visits

Coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73.

Small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent.

Customers also came back. Among Cash App users who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days.

The activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest.

Square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block said zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars.

A push for a de minimis bitcoin exemption

Block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the company said.

A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%.

Consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% said they would be more likely to pay with bitcoin if it were easier, and 15.7% of that group said they were unsure how it is taxed or regulated.

Block said Congress is weighing a crypto tax package and pointed to a de minimis exemption, which would exempt small gains on qualifying purchases, as one option. Industry groups have pressed lawmakers on crypto tax rules for months, with little movement so far.

The report doesn’t give totals. Block said the number of Square bitcoin payments, the number of sellers receiving them and total bitcoin payment volume are proprietary and not disclosed. Merchant lists like the 425 Los Angeles businesses that accept bitcoin offer a rough sense of reach.

“We think tax policy should account for how people spend bitcoin as well as how they hold it,” Block said.

Micah Zimmerman

Micah first discovered Bitcoin in 2018 but remained a skeptic on the sidelines for too long. Since 2021, he has covered crypto and business and now works as a news reporter for Bitcoin Magazine, based in North Carolina.

title: Here’s what happened in crypto today
summary: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
content:
Today in crypto, Bitcoin fell below $60,000 for the first time since July amid a broader selloff in US stocks, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde warned that differing rules could fragment Europe’s tokenized securities markets, and institutional holdings of US Bitcoin ETFs reached a record high in the third quarter.

Bitcoin falls below $60K for first time since July amid broader market selloff

Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since July, extending its recent losses amid a broader selloff in technology stocks and other risk assets.

Bitcoin (BTC) had fallen as low as $58,811 before recovering slightly to trade around $59,503, down 5.6% over the past 24 hours as of 16:52 UTC on Friday, according to CoinGecko data. The cryptocurrency has fallen 13.8% over the past week and nearly 30% over the past month.

The decline came amid a broader selloff in US equities. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.28% at 22,617.73, while the S&P 500 fell 3.69% to 6,910.77 on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance.

Shares of Anthropic (ANT), which made its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, closed down 8.50% at $88.91 amid concerns over valuations and spending in the artificial intelligence sector.

Lagarde warns Europe could miss chance to unify tokenized markets

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde warned Friday that Europe needs common rules for tokenized securities before incompatible standards take hold across trading platforms.

Speaking at the Frankfurt European Banking Congress, Lagarde said blockchain technology lets firms issue, trade and settle securities on a single platform. The global markets for tokenized assets was worth about 23 billion euros in March, five times its size a year earlier, she said.

Europe could build a single market for those assets, Lagarde said, but if platforms adopt different rules as they grow, they may be unable to settle trades with one another. She said lawmakers have a role alongside the ECB.

“Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators,” she said.

The Eurosystem launched Pontes in September, giving financial institutions a way to settle tokenized securities trades in central bank money. Earlier in November, the European Stability Mechanism used Pontes to settle a 1 billion euro (about $1.1 million) digital bond.

Through a second project, Appia, the Eurosystem is working with market participants on common standards for tokenized securities. It plans to publish a blueprint in 2028.

Institutional Bitcoin ETF holdings clock record quarter after selling streak

Institutional investment managers’ holdings of US Bitcoin exchange-traded funds climbed to a record high in the third quarter, as they reversed three straight quarters of net selling, according to regulatory filings.

The 13F filings, analyzed by Galaxy Research, show that the reporting companies added an equivalent of 49,229 Bitcoin (BTC) in the third quarter, outpacing the 47,054 Bitcoin they shed over the last three quarters combined. This lifted the reported total holdings to 356,491 BTC, the highest on record.

“The quarter’s accumulation was the work of a few dozen large institutions,” wrote Galaxy’s head of firmwide research Alex Thorn.

Quarterly 13F filings provide a point-in-time snapshot of US-listed securities held by reporting institutional investment managers. Thorn said half of the net addition of spot Bitcoin ETF shares came from advisors and wealth platforms.

title: The Hidden Cost of Prop Firms Detecting Breaches Too Late for Payouts
summary:
In proprietary trading, the most consequential failures are
rarely the ones that surface first. A denied payout is usually treated as one.
The dispute is framed as a question about the trader: did the trader break a
rule?
That framing places the failure at the wrong moment.
A rule is broken when a p...
content:
In proprietary trading, the most consequential failures are rarely the ones that surface first. A denied payout is usually treated as one. The dispute is framed as a question about the trader: did the trader break a rule?

That framing places the failure at the wrong moment.

A rule is broken when a position is opened, hedged, held through a session boundary or filled against a feed. A denial arrives weeks later, when the withdrawal is reviewed. In between, the firm either could not see the breach or chose not to look. Neither explanation sits with the trader.

London's trading industry is coming home!

A denial is a control working only if the firm acted when it first could have known. Otherwise, it is a loss the firm chose to take at the most expensive moment.

The Interval Between Breach and Denial Is the Firm's Liability

Consider what a firm does between the moment a rule is broken and the moment a payout is refused. The account stays active. It may be scaled. The challenge fee has been retained, and the trader continues to build the profit that the firm later declines to release.

Payouts are rare events. In FPFX Tech data covering more than 300,000 accounts, about 7% of traders reached one. For the firm, the payout review is therefore the single moment at which its controls meet a liability that has been accruing for weeks. It is also the moment at which the firm learns what it did not see.

Every day of the interval is a decision to carry an exposure the firm says it should not have carried. A control that finds a breach at payout time has prevented nothing. It has confirmed, at the most expensive moment, that the earlier controls did not work.

Denials Tend to Trace Back to Three Failures

The first is configuration. A trader can breach a drawdown limit because of the price source the firm chose, the session boundary it set or the fill its simulation produced. When the rule is triggered by the firm's own execution model, the breach is partly the firm's output. A denial built on it is a claim about a trader that the platform helped write.

The second is detection lag. Behaviours such as cross-account hedging, copied entries and timing-based exploitation leave a trail in trade data as they happen. Firms that review them in batches, or only when a payout is requested, discover the pattern after it has already paid for itself.

The third is indifference. In some firms, the rulebook is less an operating control than a filter applied at withdrawal, and the discretion it carries is part of the economics. Rules that bite only at the payout stage are the clearest example.

Finance Magnates reported in July 2026 that a new account structure had dropped the consistency rule and the trailing drawdown, and described the direction of travel as "toward fewer rules, faster payouts and simpler drawdown math". One operator's chief executive called the consistency rule "a payout trap".

A Denial Is Only as Strong as the Evidence Held at the Time

A denial is an assertion that a rule was broken, and it has to be proved. The proof is the firm's own record: timestamps, fills, prices, account relationships and the rule as it stood when the trade was made.

A firm that can produce that record from the moment of the breach holds a defensible position. A firm that assembles it at payout holds a reconstruction.

The difference matters most when the behaviour was concealed. Hidden coordination, shared access and engineered randomness are real, and they are the reason firms keep discretion.

They are also the cases in which the quality of the firm's data decides the outcome. Concealment may leave a signature across accounts, timing and execution . A firm that was not looking for it when it happened is unlikely to prove it afterwards.

Selective enforcement compounds the problem. A rule applied at payout but not during the life of the account looks less like a control than like a decision about whom to pay. That is the position in which a firm is least able to defend its own rulebook.

Regulated Markets Settled the Timing Question Years Ago

In US securities markets, the question of when a risk control should act was answered in 2010. The SEC's Market Access Rule requires brokers with market access to maintain controls reasonably designed to prevent the entry of orders unless regulatory requirements are met "on a pre-order entry basis", and to block orders that exceed pre-set credit or capital thresholds.

The controls must sit under the broker's "direct and exclusive control". Surveillance staff receive immediate post-trade execution reports, and the firm must review the effectiveness of its controls regularly.

The rule applies to broker-dealers, not to prop firms. Its logic is portable. A control that acts after the fact is a reporting function. A control that acts before the order or during the position is a risk control. Most prop rulebooks describe the second and operate the first.

The same diagnosis has been offered from inside the industry. James Glyde, chief executive of PipFarm, told Finance Magnates in 2024 that "most (if not all) recent prop firm failures can be traced back to a lack of internal controls".

Finance Magnates Intelligence estimates that 80 to 100 prop firms ceased operating between January 2024 and the first quarter of 2026.

Parts of the Industry Are Beginning to Move the Check Forward

Some firms are treating the problem as one of timing. On 24 August 2026, FundingTraders introduced a dashboard that shows rule breaches before a trader requests a payout, labelling each outcome as a warning, a deduction or a reduced profit split.

Finance Magnates reported that one broker had identified a single rule, profit distribution, as the source of the most disputes among its challenge clients.

Hola Prime commissioned Deloitte to review its payout processing from 15 October 2025 to 15 March 2026. The review found that 98.35% of withdrawal requests were processed within one hour and that no payouts were denied.

The firm's chief executive described a "Zero Payout Denial Policy". Figures of this kind describe the payout stage. They say less about the decisions taken before a request reaches it.

The verification problem is wider. In one reported case, a firm's monthly payout total for February 2026 and an independent tracker's estimate differed by roughly $2.2 million. In an industry that largely verifies itself, the denial decision is rarely a figure anyone outside the firm can check.

The Limits of Moving Earlier

A common counterargument is that firms need discretion at payout because some traders exploit latency, copy accounts or hedge across entities, and not all of it is visible until a withdrawal is reviewed.

That critique is valid in isolation. Behavioural detection is probabilistic, false positives carry their own cost, and no industry standard exists for what counts as sufficient evidence. It becomes less convincing as soon as the behaviour was visible in trade data for the life of the account, and in a market that records every fill, most behaviour is.

Discretion exercised at payout is defensible when the evidence emerged at payout. It is hard to defend when the evidence existed for weeks and the account was allowed to run.

The direction is clearer than the method. Rules evaluated on every event rather than every request, consequences shown to the trader while the account is live, surveillance that runs continuously, and published payout figures that reconcile against an independent record would each narrow the interval. None of them is yet common practice.

Retail prop trading also sits largely outside direct financial regulation. Finance Magnates described the arrangement as "compliance with a private contract, not oversight by a financial regulator". The firm's own process is therefore the only control the trader has, and the only one the firm can be held to.

The Question That Follows

The question is not whether firms will deny payouts. It is whether, for each denial, a firm can state the moment at which it could first have known, and what it did in the time between.

A control that works only at payout time has already failed.

In proprietary trading, the most consequential failures are rarely the ones that surface first. A denied payout is usually treated as one. The dispute is framed as a question about the trader: did the trader break a rule?

That framing places the failure at the wrong moment.

A rule is broken when a position is opened, hedged, held through a session boundary or filled against a feed. A denial arrives weeks later, when the withdrawal is reviewed. In between, the firm either could not see the breach or chose not to look. Neither explanation sits with the trader.

London's trading industry is coming home!

A denial is a control working only if the firm acted when it first could have known. Otherwise, it is a loss the firm chose to take at the most expensive moment.

The Interval Between Breach and Denial Is the Firm's Liability

Consider what a firm does between the moment a rule is broken and the moment a payout is refused. The account stays active. It may be scaled. The challenge fee has been retained, and the trader continues to build the profit that the firm later declines to release.

Payouts are rare events. In FPFX Tech data covering more than 300,000 accounts, about 7% of traders reached one. For the firm, the payout review is therefore the single moment at which its controls meet a liability that has been accruing for weeks. It is also the moment at which the firm learns what it did not see.

Every day of the interval is a decision to carry an exposure the firm says it should not have carried. A control that finds a breach at payout time has prevented nothing. It has confirmed, at the most expensive moment, that the earlier controls did not work.

Denials Tend to Trace Back to Three Failures

The first is configuration. A trader can breach a drawdown limit because of the price source the firm chose, the session boundary it set or the fill its simulation produced. When the rule is triggered by the firm's own execution model, the breach is partly the firm's output. A denial built on it is a claim about a trader that the platform helped write.

The second is detection lag. Behaviours such as cross-account hedging, copied entries and timing-based exploitation leave a trail in trade data as they happen. Firms that review them in batches, or only when a payout is requested, discover the pattern after it has already paid for itself.

The third is indifference. In some firms, the rulebook is less an operating control than a filter applied at withdrawal, and the discretion it carries is part of the economics. Rules that bite only at the payout stage are the clearest example.

Finance Magnates reported in July 2026 that a new account structure had dropped the consistency rule and the trailing drawdown, and described the direction of travel as "toward fewer rules, faster payouts and simpler drawdown math". One operator's chief executive called the consistency rule "a payout trap".

A Denial Is Only as Strong as the Evidence Held at the Time

A denial is an assertion that a rule was broken, and it has to be proved. The proof is the firm's own record: timestamps, fills, prices, account relationships and the rule as it stood when the trade was made.

A firm that can produce that record from the moment of the breach holds a defensible position. A firm that assembles it at payout holds a reconstruction.

The difference matters most when the behaviour was concealed. Hidden coordination, shared access and engineered randomness are real, and they are the reason firms keep discretion.

They are also the cases in which the quality of the firm's data decides the outcome. Concealment may leave a signature across accounts, timing and execution . A firm that was not looking for it when it happened is unlikely to prove it afterwards.

Selective enforcement compounds the problem. A rule applied at payout but not during the life of the account looks less like a control than like a decision about whom to pay. That is the position in which a firm is least able to defend its own rulebook.

Regulated Markets Settled the Timing Question Years Ago

In US securities markets, the question of when a risk control should act was answered in 2010. The SEC's Market Access Rule requires brokers with market access to maintain controls reasonably designed to prevent the entry of orders unless regulatory requirements are met "on a pre-order entry basis", and to block orders that exceed pre-set credit or capital thresholds.

The controls must sit under the broker's "direct and exclusive control". Surveillance staff receive immediate post-trade execution reports, and the firm must review the effectiveness of its controls regularly.

The rule applies to broker-dealers, not to prop firms. Its logic is portable. A control that acts after the fact is a reporting function. A control that acts before the order or during the position is a risk control. Most prop rulebooks describe the second and operate the first.

The same diagnosis has been offered from inside the industry. James Glyde, chief executive of PipFarm, told Finance Magnates in 2024 that "most (if not all) recent prop firm failures can be traced back to a lack of internal controls".

Finance Magnates Intelligence estimates that 80 to 100 prop firms ceased operating between January 2024 and the first quarter of 2026.

Parts of the Industry Are Beginning to Move the Check Forward

Some firms are treating the problem as one of timing. On 24 August 2026, FundingTraders introduced a dashboard that shows rule breaches before a trader requests a payout, labelling each outcome as a warning, a deduction or a reduced profit split.

Finance Magnates reported that one broker had identified a single rule, profit distribution, as the source of the most disputes among its challenge clients.

Hola Prime commissioned Deloitte to review its payout processing from 15 October 2025 to 15 March 2026. The review found that 98.35% of withdrawal requests were processed within one hour and that no payouts were denied.

The firm's chief executive described a "Zero Payout Denial Policy". Figures of this kind describe the payout stage. They say less about the decisions taken before a request reaches it.
